title: Trigeminal vs. Facial: Distinguishing Cluster Headache from Hemifacial Spasm
summary: A comprehensive neuro-ophthalmic deep-dive into the distinct pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management of Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias (Cluster Headache) and Seventh Nerve Hyper-excitability (Hemifacial Spasm). Essential for differential diagnosis in the eye clinic.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Core Concepts
sections.content: Cluster Headache (CH) is a primary headache disorder classified as a Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC), characterized by excruciating unilateral periorbital pain and ipsilateral cranial autonomic features. Hemifacial Spasm (HFS) is a peripherally mediated movement disorder characterized by involuntary, paroxysmal, intermittent tonic or clonic contractions of muscles innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII), typically beginning in the orbicularis oculi.

sections.title: CH: ICHD-3 Diagnostic Criteria
content: At least 5 attacks fulfilling criteria.
Severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain.
Ipsilateral conjunctival injection or lacrimation.
Ipsilateral nasal congestion or rhinorrhea.
Ipsilateral eyelid edema or forehead/facial sweating.
Ipsilateral miosis or ptosis (Horner-like).
Sense of restlessness or agitation during attack.
Attacks occur from 1 every other day to 8 per day.

rows: Mild, noticeable twitching; no functional disability
Severe, disfiguring spasm; functional blindness during event

sections.title: The Cluster Headache 'Red Flags'
content: New onset 'Cluster-like' pain in patients >50 (Rule out GCA)
Abnormal Neurological Exam between attacks (Suggests secondary cause)
Horner Syndrome that persists after the headache resolves (Carotid dissection)
Resistance to standard therapy (Consider pituitary imaging)
Atypical location (strictly occipital or lower face)

sections.title: Imaging & Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Clinical History focusing on periodicity and autonomic signs.
Step 2: MRI Brain with/without Gadolinium for all new Cluster cases (Rule out Pituitary/Sinus pathology).
Step 3: MRI/MRA with CISS/FIESTA sequences for HFS (Identify Neurovascular Conflict).
Step 4: EMG/Nerve Conduction (Identify synkinesis and 'after-discharges' in HFS).
Step 5: MRA Neck if Carotid Dissection is suspected in persistent Horner's.

content.explanation: P: Ptosis/Miosis (Sympathetic paresis), L: Lacrimation (Parasympathetic excess), U: Upper Eyelid Edema, N: Nasal Congestion, G: Gushing (Rhinorrhea).

sections.title: Management of Cluster Headache
content: Abortive: 100% Oxygen (12-15 L/min for 15 mins) via non-rebreather mask.
Abortive: Sumatriptan 6mg SC or 20mg Intranasal.
Transitional: Oral Steroids (Prednisone 60-100mg/day taper) or Greater Occipital Nerve Block.
Prophylaxis: Verapamil (First line) 240-960mg daily (Requires baseline ECG).
Prophylaxis: Lithium Carbonate (Target level 0.6-1.2 mEq/L).
Recent Advance: Galcanezumab (Emgality) 300mg SC monthly.

sections.title: Management of Hemifacial Spasm
content: First Line: Botulinum Toxin Type A (OnabotulinumtoxinA).
Injection Sites: Orbicularis oculi, corrugator, procerus, zygomaticus major.
Dosage: Typically 10-40 Units total; repeated every 3-4 months.
Pharmacotherapy: Carbamazepine or Baclofen (limited efficacy).
Definitive: Microvascular Decompression (MVD).

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Microvascular Decompression (MVD)
content: Step 1: Suboccipital craniectomy/craniotomy in the park-bench position.
Step 2: Microsurgical dissection of the cerebellopontine angle (CPA).
Step 3: Identification of the offending vessel (usually PICA or AICA) at the Root Exit Zone (REZ) of CN VII.
Step 4: Transposition of the vessel away from the nerve.
Step 5: Interposition of a non-absorbable 'cushion' (e.g., Teflon felt) between the vessel and the nerve.
Step 6: Intraoperative monitoring of 'lateral spread response' (LSR) to confirm decompression.

branches: HFS: Facial Myokymia (Continuous 'bag of worms' contraction)
HFS: Post-paralytic Synkinesis (History of Bell's Palsy)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Other' Babinski Sign: In HFS, the brow elevates during eye closure (contradictory to normal physiology).
Cluster Periodicity: Attacks often occur at the same time each day ('Alarm clock' headache).
Verapamil Safety: Always obtain an ECG to monitor for PR interval prolongation (Heart block risk).
MVD Success: Approximately 85-95% long-term cure rate for HFS.
Botox Duration: Tends to be shorter in HFS than in Blepharospasm due to muscle hyper-excitability.

rows: Chronic CH (no remission), Depression/Suicide risk, Verapamil-induced bradycardia
80% maintain episodic pattern; good response to medical prophylaxis
Facial weakness (post-Botox or MVD), Hearing loss (MVD risk), Corneal exposure
Excellent with MVD; requires lifelong Botox if surgery is declined
